summary: Defines how NETCONF, the protocol for configuring network devices, can deliver asynchronous notifications. An optional capability built on the base protocol, it specifies the operations and capabilities needed so a client can subscribe and be told about events on a device as they happen, rather than polling.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCONF is the protocol a management system uses to configure network devices. This RFC adds the other half of the job: the device tells the manager when something happens, such as a configuration change or a fault, instead of the manager asking every few minutes.

questions: how to subscribe to netconf events
what is the netconf event stream
subtitle: Letting a network device push event notices to a management client as they happen.

tldr.problem: A management system that uses NETCONF has to poll a device to find out what has changed, which wastes sessions and delays the news.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an optional capability in which the client creates a subscription, the server sends notification messages as matching events occur, and the client can narrow the flow with a filter and ask for recent events to be replayed.
tldr.outcome: The device pushes only the events the client asked for, over the same session and the same data model it already uses for configuration.

facts.label: Time format for startTime and stopTime

today: RFC 5277 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it adds an optional capability to the NETCONF protocol of RFC 4741 rather than changing it.

sections.title: What the Capability Adds
sections.content:
NETCONF can be thought of as four layers. The content layer holds configuration data. The operations layer holds the operations that act on it, such as get-config, edit-config and notification. The RPC layer holds the request and reply elements that carry those operations, and the transport layer is the protocol underneath, such as BEEP, SSH, SSL or a console.

This document defines mechanisms that provide an asynchronous message notification delivery service for the NETCONF protocol. It is an optional capability built on top of the base NETCONF definition, and it defines the capabilities and operations needed to support the service.

The motivation is to allow asynchronous messages that are consistent with the data model and the security model already used inside a NETCONF implementation. The scope aims at a list of operational needs: the first release should support notifications for configuration operations; the same data model should serve both notifications and configuration operations; the solution should support a reasonable message size limit rather than a very short one; the notifications should travel over a connection-oriented mechanism; there should be a subscription mechanism, taking into account that a server does not send notifications before being asked and that the client starts the flow; there should be a filtering mechanism inside the server; the information in a notification should be enough to analyse it without knowing the transport, so that the data content fully describes the notification; and the server should be able to replay locally logged notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is used to configure devices, and it is built in layers: the data, the operations on the data, the request and reply format, and the transport. This RFC adds a layer of operations that push events to the manager, using the same data model and the same security rules as the rest of NETCONF.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
An element is an XML element. A subscription is an agreement and a method to receive event notifications over a NETCONF session, involving the destination of the notifications and the selection of them; it is bound to the lifetime of a session. An operation is a NETCONF protocol operation, and within this document it means one of the operations defined to support notifications.

An event is something that happens that may be of interest, such as a configuration change, a fault, a change in status, crossing a threshold or an external input to the system. Often this results in an asynchronous message, called a notification or an event notification, being sent to interested parties.

Replay is the ability to send, or resend, previously logged notifications on request; those notifications are sent asynchronously, the feature is implemented by the server and invoked by the client. A stream is a set of event notifications matching some forwarding criteria, available to clients for subscription. A filter is a parameter that says which subset of all possible events are of interest, defined as one or more filter elements, each of which identifies a part of the overall filter.
sections.plainLanguage: The words to learn are subscription, which is the client's standing request to be told about events, and stream, which is a named group of events that the device offers. A filter narrows what the client receives within a stream.

sections.title: Creating and Ending a Subscription
sections.content:
The client indicates its interest by creating a subscription, and the server replies to say whether the request succeeded. If it did, the server begins sending notifications as the events occur, and it keeps doing so until the NETCONF session ends or the subscription ends for some other reason. The subscription lets the client say which events it wants, and those choices are made when the subscription is created: a subscription cannot be modified afterwards.

The subscription is initiated by the client, responded to by the server, and is bound to a single stream for its lifetime. The operation takes four optional parameters. The stream parameter names the stream of events of interest; without it, events from the default NETCONF stream are sent. The filter parameter indicates which subset of all possible events is of interest, in the same format as the filter parameter of the NETCONF protocol operations; without it, all events not precluded by other parameters are sent. The startTime parameter triggers the replay feature and says when the replay should start; it is of type dateTime and compliant with RFC 3339, and implementations must support time zones. It is not valid to give a start time later than the current time, and if the start time is earlier than the log can support, the replay begins with the earliest available notification. The stopTime parameter says the newest notifications of interest; it must be used with a startTime and be later than it, and a value in the future is valid.

If the server can satisfy the request it sends an ok element. If it cannot, the reply carries an rpc-error element, and the request fails when the filter has invalid syntax or the name of a stream that does not exist is given. A stopTime without a startTime gives the error tag missing-element. Asking for replay when the server does not support it gives the tag operation-failed. A stopTime earlier than the startTime, or a startTime later than the current time, gives the tag bad-element.

Once the subscription is set up, the server sends the notifications asynchronously over the connection. A notification is a complete and well-formed XML document, sent when an event of interest has occurred, and it is not an RPC method but the top-level element identifying a one-way message. It carries the time the event was generated by the event source, of type dateTime and compliant with RFC 3339, and any notification-specific tagged content; apart from the event time, that content is beyond the scope of the document. There is no response to a notification.

The subscription can end in several ways: the client can close it with the close-session operation, the NETCONF session can be terminated with kill-session, or the underlying transport session can be terminated from another session. If a stop time was given when the subscription was created, the subscription ends when that time is reached, and the NETCONF session is still active afterwards. The server must accept and process close-session even while a subscription is active. It may accept and process other commands; if it does not, those are rejected with a resource-denied error, and the server says that it can handle them with the interleave capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a request to subscribe, naming the stream it wants, an optional filter, and optionally the time range to replay. The server answers yes or no with a reason. From then on the server pushes notification messages, each a complete XML document saying when the event happened and what it was. The subscription ends when the client closes the session, when the session is killed, or when a stop time is reached.

sections.title: Event Streams and How Events Are Distributed
sections.content:
An event stream is a set of event notifications matching some forwarding criteria. The document draws the flow of notifications in a figure, and does not mandate or preclude any implementation by it. System components generate event notifications that are passed to a central component for classification and distribution. That central component inspects each notification and matches it against the set of stream definitions; when a match occurs the notification is a member of that stream, and one notification may be part of several streams.

After the server receives an internal event from a stream, it is converted to an XML encoding, and a notification element is ready to send to all the sessions subscribed to that stream. Access control is then applied by the server: if a session has no permission to receive the notification, it is discarded for that session and the processing of the internal event is complete for that session.

When a client subscribes to a stream, user-defined filter elements are applied to the stream, and the matching notifications are forwarded for distribution to the subscribed clients. The filter travels from the client to the server in the subscription operation and is applied against each notification element generated by the stream. A notification logging service may also be available, in which case the central component logs notifications and the server can later retrieve logged ones through the replay feature.

Event streams are predefined on the managed device, and configuring them is outside the scope of the document, but they are expected to be pre-established by the vendor, user configurable as part of the device's configuration, or both. The contents of all streams made available to a client must be encoded in XML. A server that supports the capability must support the default NETCONF stream, which contains all the NETCONF XML event notifications the server supports, and the exact string NETCONF is what appears in the advertisement of stream support and in the subscription operation. Sources other than the default stream, such as SNMP or syslog, are outside the scope of the document, though an implementation may use any source it likes when creating streams.

A client finds the streams it may use with the get operation, asking for the streams subtree. The reply holds a name element for each stream, which is mandatory and unique within the scope of the server, and a description element, and it may also say whether replay is supported and, if so, the timestamp of the earliest notification that can be replayed.
sections.plainLanguage: The device collects events from its own components, sorts them into named streams, and applies each subscriber's filter. Anything a subscriber is not allowed to see is dropped for that subscriber alone. The client asks the device which streams it can have, and the answer lists them with a name and a description.

sections.title: Replay and Filtering
sections.content:
Replay is the ability to create a subscription that resends recently generated notifications, or in some cases sends them for the first time to a particular client. Those notifications are sent the same way as normal ones. A replay is requested by including the optional startTime parameter, which gives the start of the replay, and the optional stopTime parameter, which gives the end. If stopTime is absent, notifications continue until the subscription is terminated. Both times refer to the time the event was generated by the event source, not the time it was sent.

A stream that supports replay is not expected to hold an unlimited supply of saved notifications. Clients can ask for the replay log creation time and the replay log aged time to learn what is available, and the number of stored notifications is an implementation matter outside the scope of the document. Whether a stream supports replay can be discovered with a get operation on the streams element and a look at the replaySupport value, and the same schema provides the replayLogCreationTime element that gives the earliest available logged notification.

A replayComplete notification is sent to say that all the replay notifications have been sent, and it must not be sent for any other reason. If the subscription has a stop time, the session returns to being a normal command-response session once the replay and the following notificationComplete have been sent.

Filtering is stated when the subscription is created, through the filter parameter, and a filter exists only as a parameter to a subscription. If a filter looks for data of a particular value and that data item is not present in a notification, the notification is filtered out, so a filter looking for severity=critical drops a configuration notification that has no severity field. For subtree filtering, a non-empty node set means that the filter matches; for XPath filtering, the mechanisms of XPath are used to convert the returned value to a boolean. Either subtree or XPath filtering can be used, and XPath support for the notification capability is advertised as part of the normal XPath capability advertisement.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscription can ask for events that happened earlier by giving a start time, and the server sends the logged ones first, then says when the replay is finished with a replayComplete notification. A filter is set once, when the subscription is made, and a notification that does not contain the value the filter looks for is dropped.

sections.title: The Interleave Capability
sections.content:
The interleave capability says that the peer supports interleaving other NETCONF operations inside a notification subscription. That means the NETCONF server must receive, process and respond to NETCONF requests on a session that has an active subscription. The capability helps scalability, because fewer NETCONF sessions are needed for a given operator or management application.

The capability depends on the notification capability being supported, and it is identified by the string urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:interleave:1.0. It defines no new operations. It does change one existing operation: when a create-subscription is sent while another subscription is already active on that session, the server returns the error with the tag operation-failed, of error type protocol and severity error.
sections.plainLanguage: Without the interleave capability, a session that has a subscription running can do almost nothing else. With it, the client can still send ordinary requests on the same session while the notifications keep coming, so a manager needs fewer sessions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the base NETCONF document also apply to the notification capability, and the access control framework and the choice of transport have a major impact on the security of the solution. Notification elements are never sent before the transport layer and the NETCONF layer, including the capabilities exchange, have been established and the manager has been identified and authenticated.

The document recommends care in three places: the invocation of create-subscription, the get operation on read-only data models, and the content of notifications. Secure execution means using a secure transport and making sure the user is authorized for the function they are requesting against the subset of NETCONF content involved. When a get is received that refers to the content defined in this document, clients should only see the content for which they have sufficient privileges. A create-subscription operation can be considered like a deferred get, and the content different users can reach may vary, which is reflected in the notifications different users are able to subscribe to.

One potential issue is the transport of data from non-NETCONF streams, such as syslog and SNMP. Such data may be more vulnerable, or less vulnerable, when carried over NETCONF than when carried by the protocol normally used for it, depending on the security credentials of the two subsystems, and the NETCONF server is responsible for applying access control to stream content. The contents of notifications, and the names of the streams, may hold sensitive information, so they should be seen only by authorised users, and the server must not include any content in a notification that the user is not authorised to view.

If a subscription was created with a stopTime, the session returns to being a normal command-response session when the replay is complete, and it is the client's job to close that session when it is no longer needed. Finally, a malicious or buggy client that sends a number of create-subscription requests can make the subscriptions accumulate and use up system resources, and in that situation the subscriptions can be terminated by killing the suspect underlying sessions with the kill-session operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing is sent until the session is secure and the manager has been identified. What a subscriber receives depends on what that manager is allowed to see, and the server has to enforce that for each stream, including streams whose events came from another protocol such as syslog. A client that asks for too many subscriptions can be cut off by killing its sessions.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers three URIs in the IETF XML registry. The first two are capability identifiers: the notification capability is urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:notification:1.0 and the interleave capability is urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:interleave:1.0. The other two are XML namespaces, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:notification and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:notification:1.0, with the IESG as the registrant contact. IANA also registered the XML schema defined in Section 4 of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to register two names that say which capabilities a device supports, and two XML namespaces that the messages live in.

WHAT A SUBSCRIPTION CAN ASK FOR

items.title: stream
items.text: Which stream of events is of interest. The default NETCONF stream is used if it is absent.

items.title: filter
items.text: Which subset of the events in that stream is of interest, in the same format as the NETCONF filter.

items.title: startTime
items.text: Triggers the replay and says when it should start. It cannot be later than the current time.

items.title: stopTime
items.text: Says the newest notification of interest. It must be used with startTime and must be later.
